root.overview: The Artificial Intelligence Governance Professional (AIGP) is the IAPP's certification for professionals who ensure AI systems are developed, deployed, and managed responsibly and in line with law, policy, and emerging standards. It is deliberately cross-disciplinary: the Body of Knowledge spans foundational AI concepts, the global legal and regulatory landscape, and hands-on governance of the AI lifecycle from design through retirement.
root.exam: The exam draws from four domains with fixed question-count ranges, so preparation effort should roughly mirror those weights: Domains III and IV (governing AI development, deployment, and use) together carry about half the exam, while Domain I (foundations) and Domain II (laws, standards, and frameworks) carry the rest. Scenario questions dominate — expect to apply governance judgment to realistic situations, not just recall definitions.
key_points: Four BOK domains: I Foundations of AI Governance, II Laws/Standards/Frameworks, III Governing AI Development, IV Governing AI Deployment & Use
The exam favors applied judgment: 'what should the governance professional do NEXT' scenarios over rote definitions
Core recurring themes across every domain: risk-based proportionality, human oversight, documentation, transparency, and accountability

The heavyweight reference texts (BOK v2.1) are the EU AI Act, GDPR, the NIST AI RMF and Playbook, ISO/IEC 22989, 42001 and 42005, and the OECD AI Principles — plus the South Korean AI Basic Act and US federal/state AI laws for II.C
When two answers both look right, prefer the one that is risk-based, documented, and multidisciplinary — that pattern resolves a large share of hard questions

d2.overview: Domain II maps the external rulebook: the laws that already reach AI (GDPR, non-discrimination, IP, consumer protection, product liability), AI-specific laws — the EU AI Act as the first comprehensive AI statute, plus South Korea's AI Basic Act and US federal and state AI laws (added in BOK v2.1) — and the voluntary standards and frameworks (OECD, NIST, ISO) that organizations use to operationalize trustworthy AI. The skill being tested is knowing which instrument applies to which situation, and what it actually requires.
d2.exam: The second-heaviest domain at roughly 19–23 questions. The EU AI Act is the single most-tested instrument — risk tiers, prohibited practices, high-risk obligations, GPAI rules, penalties, and the implementation timeline all appear. GDPR questions focus on its AI pressure points: Article 22 automated decisions, special categories, DPIAs, and data subject rights against models.
key_points: Spans four knowledge areas: privacy/data protection law, sectoral and civil laws, AI-specific laws (EU AI Act, Korea AI Basic Act, US federal/state AI laws), and AI standards & frameworks
EU AI Act risk ladder: unacceptable (banned) → high-risk (heavy obligations) → limited (transparency) → minimal (largely unregulated)
Penalty anchors: €35M/7% for prohibited practices, €15M/3% for high-risk non-compliance, €7.5M/1% for misleading information
Existing law reaches AI even without 'AI' in its name: ECOA and Title VII for discrimination, FTC Act for deception, product liability for defects
Standards stack: OECD principles (values) → NIST AI RMF (risk process) → ISO/IEC 42001 (certifiable management system) → ISO/IEC 23894 (risk guidance)

d3.overview: Domain III governs the build: planning and designing an AI system, assessing its impacts before committing, governing the data that feeds it, and testing the resulting models for performance, robustness, fairness, security, and explainability. Its center of gravity is evidence — documented lifecycles, lineage, impact assessments, and test results that prove the system was built deliberately.
d3.exam: Roughly 21–25 questions. Expect deep scenario testing on data governance (lawful sourcing, quality, representativeness), the testing taxonomy (unit, integration, validation, performance, security, bias, adversarial), and impact assessments. Questions often hinge on sequencing — what must happen before training, before testing, before release.
key_points: Spans AI system design, data governance & model training, and pre-deployment work
Documentation artifacts to know: model cards, datasheets, system cards, impact assessments, risk registers
Data governance pillars: lawful authority to use data, quality, representativeness, lineage/provenance, minimization, security
Testing must cover more than accuracy: robustness (edge cases), fairness (across groups), security (poisoning, inversion, adversarial examples), explainability
Overfitting/underfitting, drift, and representativeness failures are the recurring technical failure modes governance must catch

d4.overview: Domain IV governs the running system: deciding it is ready to deploy, monitoring it in production, managing risks and incidents, auditing and assurance, maintaining business records, communicating externally, and eventually retiring it responsibly. The unifying idea is that governance does not end at launch — it intensifies.
d4.exam: Roughly 21–25 questions. Scenarios dominate: degraded accuracy discovered by monitoring, incidents requiring disclosure, audits finding gaps, systems needing rollback or retirement. The tested instinct is continuous verification — monitor, investigate root causes, document, remediate, communicate — rather than one-time signoff.
key_points: Spans risk management & assurance, incident management, ongoing operations, and retirement
Post-deployment monitoring spans performance, drift, fairness, security, and usage patterns — not just uptime
Incident management lifecycle: detect → contain → investigate root cause → remediate → disclose as required → feed lessons back
The EU AI Act mandates post-market monitoring and serious-incident reporting for high-risk systems
Retirement is a governance event: notify stakeholders, honor data obligations, preserve required records, prevent orphaned dependencies

ch4.overview: This knowledge area applies privacy and data protection law to AI. Core doctrines — notice, choice, consent, purpose limitation, data minimization, privacy by design — collide with AI's appetite for repurposed data and its ability to infer what was never collected. It also covers controller obligations (lawful basis, DPIAs, processor contracts), special categories of data, and the data subject rights that now reach into models.
ch4.exam: GDPR is the reference statute: Article 22 (automated decision-making), Article 9 (special categories), Article 35 (DPIAs), Article 28 (processor contracts). Scenario questions test whether processing needs consent or another lawful basis, when a DPIA is mandatory, and what secondary use of data for training requires.
key_points: Purpose limitation is AI's chronic pain point: data collected for service delivery cannot be silently repurposed for model training
Data minimization applies to models too — if 15 features perform like 50, use 15
GDPR Article 22 grants the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal/significant effects, with narrow exceptions and required safeguards
DPIAs are required for high-risk processing — systematic profiling, large-scale special categories — and AI routinely triggers them
Special categories (health, biometrics, race, etc.) need an Article 9 condition; beware AI inferring special-category data from ordinary inputs
Controllers must bind processors with Article 28 DPAs: documented instructions, security, sub-processor controls, audit rights

ch5.overview: This knowledge area surveys the sectoral and civil laws that reach AI without naming it: intellectual property (training-data copyright, output ownership, trade secrets), non-discrimination law (disparate impact through proxies), consumer protection (deception and unfairness), and product liability (defective AI as a product). The lesson is that 'no AI law here' never means 'no law here.'
ch5.exam: Scenario-heavy: an AI credit model with disparate impact (ECOA/fair lending), a chatbot making deceptive claims (FTC Act), a generative model trained on copyrighted works (fair use fight), an autonomous product causing injury (strict liability vs. negligence). Match the fact pattern to the doctrine.
key_points: Copyright: training on protected works raises unresolved fair-use questions; purely AI-generated output lacks copyright without human authorship
Disparate impact doctrine catches facially neutral models that harm protected classes through proxy variables (zip code → race)
Key US anti-discrimination hooks: Title VII (employment), ECOA (credit), Fair Housing Act (housing)
FTC Act §5 reaches AI: deceptive claims about AI capabilities, unfair algorithmic practices, and dark patterns
Product liability theories against AI: manufacturing defect, design defect, failure to warn — strict liability doesn't require proving negligence

ch6.label: II.C · AI-Specific Laws
ch6.overview: BOK v2.1 II.C covers the main elements of AI-specific laws. The EU AI Act is the anchor: risk tiers (prohibited, high, limited, minimal), a heavy compliance chain for high-risk systems, transparency duties, a separate GPAI regime, role-based obligations and GDPR-scale penalties. Under v2.1 the subdomain also covers South Korea's AI Basic Act and US federal and state AI laws that apply to private-sector organisations. The EU AI Act itself was amended by the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026), which moved the high-risk dates and simplified several duties.
ch6.exam: 6–8 questions (up from 5–7 under v2.0.1). Expect tier classification, the high-risk obligations chain, GPAI vs. systemic-risk GPAI duties, provider/deployer/importer/distributor splits and the penalty ladder, plus comparisons across jurisdictions. Date items may follow the original AI Act text, so learn both the 'as enacted' and 'as amended' timelines.
key_points: Risk tiers: prohibited (Art. 5), high-risk (Annex I products and Annex III uses), limited-risk transparency (Art. 50), minimal risk
Prohibitions: eight as enacted, from 2 Feb 2025; the 2026 Omnibus adds intimate-imagery and CSAM bans from 2 Dec 2026

High-risk provider chain: risk management, data governance, documentation, logging, instructions, human oversight, accuracy and security, QMS, conformity assessment, CE mark, registration, post-market monitoring

GPAI: all providers owe documentation, downstream information, a copyright policy and a training-content summary; systemic-risk models (presumed above 10^25 FLOP) add evaluations, risk mitigation, incident reporting and cybersecurity
Penalties: €35m/7% for prohibitions; €15m/3% for most obligations and Commission GPAI fines; €7.5m/1% for misleading information; lower-figure caps for SMEs, and for SMCs in the two lower tiers
Timeline as amended: Art. 50 and GPAI enforcement 2 Aug 2026; Annex III high-risk 2 Dec 2027; Annex I high-risk 2 Aug 2028
Beyond the EU: II.C now includes South Korea's AI Basic Act and US federal and state AI laws; compare their risk tiers, roles and enforcement

ch7.overview: This knowledge area tours the voluntary standards and frameworks that turn principles into practice: the OECD AI Principles (the intergovernmental values baseline, with its classification framework and AI-system definition), NIST's AI RMF with its Govern-Map-Measure-Manage cycle and the Playbook's per-subcategory suggested actions, the Generative AI Profile, and the three ISO standards BOK v2.1 names — 22989 (terminology), 42001 (certifiable AI management system) and 42005 (AI system impact assessment). None are law, but regulators, auditors, and contracts increasingly treat them as the de facto duty of care.
ch7.exam: 3–5 questions under BOK v2.1. Match the instrument to its function: values → OECD; risk process → NIST AI RMF; how-to actions → the Playbook; vocabulary → ISO 22989; certifiable management system → ISO 42001; impact assessment of a specific system → ISO 42005. NIST ARIA was removed in v2.1, and ISO 23894 is not named.
key_points: OECD AI Principles (2019, revised 2024): first intergovernmental AI standard; the 2023 AI-system definition and the 2022 classification framework sit alongside
NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023): voluntary, non-certifiable; Govern → Map → Measure → Manage; seven trustworthiness characteristics
NIST AI RMF Playbook: suggested actions, documentation prompts and references for all 72 subcategories — named in the BOK
ISO/IEC 42001: the certifiable AI management system (AIMS) — Annex SL structure, PDCA, the audit/certification target
ISO/IEC 42005: guidance (not certifiable) for assessing a specific AI system's impacts on people and society; complements 42001
ISO/IEC 22989 defines the shared vocabulary; 23894 (AI risk management) is background only in v2.1, as is NIST ARIA

ch8.overview: This knowledge area governs design: documenting the AI lifecycle from the first use-case conversation, grounding systems in business context and defined success criteria, running impact assessments before resources are committed, making design choices that embed governance (architecture, human oversight points, explainability), identifying design-phase risks, and handling the special constraints of proprietary and third-party models.
ch8.exam: Sequencing questions are common — impact assessment before build, success criteria before model selection. Know the documentation artifacts (model cards, datasheets, AIIAs) and what each captures, and expect scenarios about design choices that trade accuracy against explainability or privacy.
key_points: Document from day one: use case, intended users, success criteria, assumptions, exclusions — the lifecycle record starts at conception
Model cards document a model's intended use, training data, metrics, and limitations; datasheets do the same for datasets
AI impact assessments (AIIAs) evaluate social, ethical, legal, and operational impacts before and during development
Design-phase risk work is the cheapest risk work: changing an architecture costs less than remediating a deployed system
Proprietary/third-party models constrain governance: limited visibility into training data demands compensating contractual and testing controls

ch9.overview: This knowledge area covers the data and the training: establishing data governance for AI (lawful authority, quality, representativeness, stewardship, security), tracking lineage and provenance so every model output can be traced to its inputs, and the full AI testing taxonomy — unit, integration, validation, performance, security, bias/fairness, explainability, human-in-the-loop — plus the testing risks that remain even when everything passes.
ch9.exam: The most technical knowledge area and it shows on the exam: expect questions on overfitting vs. underfitting, representativeness failures, drift, train/validation/test splits, and which test type catches which failure. 'It passed testing' is never the right final answer — testing risks and residual risk management follow.
key_points: Data governance for AI: confirm lawful rights to use data (including secondary use), quality dimensions, fit-for-purpose checks, stewardship roles
Representativeness: training data must reflect the deployment population — its absence is the root of most bias findings
Lineage tracks data's journey through transformations; provenance records its origin — both are prerequisites for audit and incident response
Testing taxonomy: unit → integration → validation → performance → security (poisoning, inversion, adversarial) → bias/fairness → explainability → HITL/scenario
Overfitting memorizes noise (great train, poor real-world); underfitting misses the signal entirely; both are data-sufficiency red flags
Testing risks persist post-pass: coverage gaps, benchmark gaming, distribution shift between test and production

ch10.overview: This knowledge area moves the system into the world: pre-release readiness (conformity, stress testing, red-teaming, formal reviews, go/no-go gates), deployment strategy choices (phased rollout, canary, A/B, shadow mode, on-prem vs. cloud), and the continuous monitoring regime that watches performance, drift, fairness, and security once real users and real data arrive.
ch10.exam: Deployment-strategy vocabulary is tested directly (canary vs. phased vs. shadow), and monitoring scenarios are a staple: accuracy degrades, drift is detected, or users behave unexpectedly — the right answer investigates root causes and follows the escalation path, never 'keep running as-is.'
key_points: Pre-release readiness: model cards complete, conformity assessments done, stress and adversarial testing passed, formal risk/impact reviews signed off
Deployment strategies manage blast radius: canary (small % first), phased rollout (expanding cohorts), shadow mode (parallel, non-authoritative), A/B
Data drift = input distribution shifts; concept drift = input→output relationship shifts; monitoring must catch both
Monitor beyond accuracy: latency, fairness across groups, security anomalies, usage patterns, and over-reliance signals
Alert thresholds, escalation paths, rollback criteria, and retraining triggers should be defined before launch, not improvised after

ch11.overview: This knowledge area is assurance: forecasting and managing AI risk with registers, tolerance, and treatment decisions; auditing and testing systems (internal and external, against frameworks like the AI RMF or ISO 42001); and running incident management — detection, containment, root-cause analysis, remediation, and the disclosure obligations that increasingly attach to AI failures.
ch11.exam: Risk-vocabulary precision pays: likelihood, impact, residual risk, risk appetite vs. tolerance. Audit questions test independence and evidence; incident scenarios test the lifecycle order and when disclosure duties (EU AI Act serious incidents, breach laws) trigger.
key_points: Risk register discipline: identified risks with owner, likelihood, impact, treatment (mitigate/transfer/avoid/accept), and residual risk vs. tolerance
Audits need independence, defined criteria (framework or standard), evidence, and tracked remediation — 'we reviewed ourselves informally' fails
Incident lifecycle: detect (monitoring, user reports, media) → contain → investigate root cause → remediate → disclose → institutionalize lessons
EU AI Act requires serious-incident reporting for high-risk systems; privacy breach laws add parallel clocks when personal data is involved
Assurance stacks: internal monitoring → internal audit → external audit/certification (e.g., ISO 42001) → regulator scrutiny

ch12.overview: This knowledge area closes the lifecycle: maintaining the business records that prove governance happened (decisions, tests, approvals, incidents — with retention schedules), communicating about AI externally (transparency reports, user notices, marketing claims that must survive FTC scrutiny), and retiring systems deliberately — decommissioning plans, data disposition, stakeholder notice, and preserving records after the system is gone.
ch12.exam: Underrated but reliably tested territory. Records questions hinge on 'if it isn't documented, it didn't happen' plus retention obligations; retirement scenarios test the checklist — notify, honor data obligations, archive records, kill dependencies — versus just switching the system off.
key_points: Records to keep: design decisions, data lineage, test results, approvals, monitoring logs, incidents, and model versions — aligned to retention schedules
The EU AI Act expects logs and technical documentation retained (10 years for high-risk providers) after market placement
External communications must be accurate: overstated AI claims are deception exposure; transparency reports build defensible trust
Retirement checklist: decommissioning plan, stakeholder notification, data return/deletion per obligations, record archival, dependency wind-down
Deactivation policies should predefine the triggers (risk, obsolescence, regulation) so retirement is a governed decision, not an emergency
